final.final_answer:
From the tutorial and go.mod reference pages on go.dev:

Verified tutorial: "Call your code from another module" (linked from "Tutorial: Create a module")
Commands used in the tutorial to:
- Initialize the caller module:
  - `go mod init example.com/hello`
  (Shown in the tutorial code and confirmed in the previously visible go.mod: `module example.com/hello`.)

- Add a local dependency using a replace directive (via go mod edit):
  - `go mod edit -replace example.com/greetings=../greetings`
  (This corresponds to the go.mod content shown in the tutorial: `replace example.com/greetings => ../greetings`.)

- Tidy dependencies:
  - `go mod tidy`
  (The tutorial showed this command and its effect: it added a `require example.com/greetings v0.0.0-…` entry to go.mod.)

- Run the program:
  - `go run .`
  (Used in the tutorial to run the example in the caller module.)

These four commands were taken directly from the tutorial pages under https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/create-module and https://go.dev/doc/tutorial/call-module-code (the latter being the "Call your code from another module" step of the multi-part tutorial).

Verified reference: go.mod file reference – replace directive
Current page: https://go.dev/doc/modules/gomod-ref#replace

Section heading: "replace"

1) Purpose (from the visible Notes text)
- "Replaces the content of a module at a specific version (or all versions) with another module version or with a local directory. Go tools will use the replacement path when resolving the dependency."

2) Syntax forms (from the "replace" section’s Syntax text)
The page gives a single general syntax that covers two forms:

General syntax line:
- `replace module-path [module-version] => replacement-path [replacement-version]`

Concretely, this expands into two distinct syntactic patterns:

a) Replacing with another module path and explicit version
   - Form: `replace module-path [module-version] => replacement-path replacement-version`
   - Constraints spelled out in the text:
     - If `replacement-path` is a module path, you must specify a `replacement-version` value.
     - Example from the page under "Replacing with a fork of the module repository":
       - `require example.com/othermodule v1.2.3`
       - `replace example.com/othermodule => example.com/myfork/othermodule v1.2.3-fixed`
     - Example under "Replacing with a different version number":
       - `require example.com/othermodule v1.2.2`
       - `replace example.com/othermodule => example.com/othermodule v1.2.3`
       - `replace example.com/othermodule v1.2.5 => example.com/othermodule v1.2.3`

b) Replacing with a local directory on the file system
   - Form: `replace module-path [module-version] => replacement-path`
   - Constraints from the reference text:
     - "If this is a local path, you may not use a replacement-version value."
     - So the form is just a path, with no trailing version.
     - Examples from "Replacing with local code":
       - `require example.com/othermodule v1.2.3`
       - `replace example.com/othermodule => ../othermodule`
       - `require example.com/othermodule v1.2.5`
       - `replace example.com/othermodule v1.2.5 => ../othermodule`

Summarizing the two syntax forms explicitly referenced in the task:
- Form 1 (module → other module, with version):
  - `replace module-path [module-version] => replacement-module-path replacement-version`
- Form 2 (module → local directory, no version on the right):
  - `replace module-path [module-version] => ./local/dir` (or another filesystem path; no `replacement-version` allowed).

3) Whether a replace directive alone adds a module to the dependency graph
The "Notes" section for replace (visible on this page) states:
- "Note that a replace directive alone does not add a module to the module graph. A require directive that refers to a replaced module version is also needed, either in the main module’s go.mod file or a dependency’s go.mod file. If you don’t have a specific version to replace, you can use a fake version, as in the example below. Note that this will break modules that depend on your module, since replace directives are only applied in the main module."
- Example immediately following that text:
  - `require example.com/mod v0.0.0-replace`
  - `replace example.com/mod v0.0.0-replace => ./mod`

So, as explicitly stated by the documentation:
- A `replace` directive by itself does not add a module to the module graph.
- To participate in the graph, the module must also appear in a `require` directive (possibly using a fake version such as `v0.0.0-replace`), and the replace then redirects where that required module’s code is found.

Final consolidated answer
- Tutorial commands (from the Go documentation tutorial pages):
  - Initialize a module: `go mod init example.com/hello`
  - Add a local dependency using replace: `go mod edit -replace example.com/greetings=../greetings`
  - Tidy dependencies: `go mod tidy`
  - Run the program: `go run .`

- replace directive reference (from https://go.dev/doc/modules/gomod-ref#replace):
  - General syntax: `replace module-path [module-version] => replacement-path [replacement-version]`
  - Two concrete syntax forms:
    1) With another module path and version: `replace module-path [module-version] => replacement-module-path replacement-version` (must specify `replacement-version` when `replacement-path` is a module path).
    2) With a local directory: `replace module-path [module-version] => ./local/dir` (or other local path; must not specify `replacement-version` when `replacement-path` is a local directory).
  - Effect on module graph: The documentation explicitly states that "a replace directive alone does not add a module to the module graph"; a corresponding `require` directive referring to the replaced module version is also necessary for the module to appear in the dependency graph.
